title: Store manager

manager.name: Hana
manager.title: Regional Manager
manager.persona_note: Hana is new to hiring. A good recruiter guides gently and explains as they go.

teaser: Hana was just promoted and is hiring for the very first time.
context: The company sells outdoor clothing and has 12 stores.
The new manager will run one store with about 15 staff.
message: Hi! I was just promoted, and this is my first time hiring. A bit nervous!
I found an old ad. Can we talk for 10 minutes?
ad: 3 or more years managing a store
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Hana will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to hire, train and keep a new store team.
needs.n2: Someone to grow the store's online sales.
needs.n3: Someone to manage stock and orders.

beats.label: First time
beats.sam: Hi! I was just promoted and this is my first time hiring anyone. Where do I even start?

choices.text: Congratulations on the promotion. Would it help if we started with what the store needs most right now?
choices.reply: Yes, thank you. That's a relief. Honestly, the store needs someone who can train brand-new staff.
choices.why: A manager hiring for the first time needs a guide before the hard questions, and starting with the store's needs is a gentle way in.

choices.text: What do you think the store needs most from a new manager right now?
choices.reply: I'm honestly not sure. That's why I'm asking.
choices.why: It's a good question, but asked straight away it adds pressure to someone who's new to this.

choices.text: Have you had any training on hiring yet?
choices.why: Questions like that can make a new manager feel judged, and they'll share less.

beats.label: Like me
beats.sam: I guess they should be a bit like me?

choices.text: That's a good place to start. What made you successful when you ran a store?
choices.reply: I kept my team. People stayed with me for years.
choices.why: Asking what made them successful turns 'like me' into a real skill to look for.

choices.text: Should I look for people with a background similar to yours?
choices.why: Hiring for a similar background can miss what this particular store needs.

choices.text: Would hiring people like yourself limit the team, do you think?
choices.why: The point is fair, but put that way it embarrasses a new manager.

choices.text: What's been the hardest thing about this store lately?
choices.reply: Staff keep quitting. We've lost six people this year.
choices.why: A gentle follow-up finds the real problem the new manager has to solve.

choices.text: Has it mostly been sales that's been difficult, or something else at the store?
choices.why: A leading guess missed it, and a new manager may not correct you.

choices.text: Why do you think the last manager struggled?
choices.why: Questions about blame make a new manager anxious, and they won't help the search.

beats.label: The degree
beats.sam: Should I ask for a retail degree?

choices.text: Did you need one to get where you are?
choices.reply: No! I worked my way up.
choices.why: Asking about their own path shows the degree isn't needed, and teaches the lesson gently.

choices.text: It probably wouldn't hurt to ask for a retail degree in the posting, would it?
choices.why: It can hurt: it would screen out strong people who, like Hana, worked their way up.

choices.text: Most managers have degrees these days, don't they?
choices.why: A leading question taught the wrong lesson to someone who's still learning.

beats.label: Interviews
beats.sam: Do I need to interview everyone who applies?

choices.text: Not at all. What would help you decide who's worth meeting?
choices.reply: Knowing who's kept a team together before.
choices.why: Answering simply, then teaching through a question, helps a new manager learn the process.

choices.text: Would you like to meet everyone, just to be fair?
choices.reply: I suppose I should, to be fair.
choices.why: That isn't necessary, and it would swamp a busy new manager.

choices.text: Wouldn't that be a big mistake with a busy store to run?
choices.why: Correcting without explaining doesn't teach a new manager anything, and it may make them hesitate to ask.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: I'm actually not sure what the pay is.

choices.text: That's completely normal. Who could we check with to confirm the range?
choices.reply: HR. I'll ask them today. I think it's $58,000 to $65,000.
choices.why: Helping a new manager find the answer teaches them the process.

choices.text: We'll really need that before we start. Could you find out today?
choices.why: It's true, but it felt like pressure to someone who's new to all of this.

choices.text: No problem. Shall we just figure it out later?
choices.why: Agreeing means you'd search without a budget, and that causes problems later.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Weekends
beats.sam: Weekends are part of the job. Is that okay?

choices.text: That's normal in retail, and candidates will expect it. Shall I mention it early on?
choices.why: A quick yes on a normal detail reassures a new manager and keeps things clear for candidates.

choices.text: Is it every single weekend, or more like a rotation with the rest of the team?
choices.why: It's fine to ask, but it isn't needed right now and doesn't change the search.

choices.text: Won't weekend work make the role hard to fill?
choices.why: Adding worry doesn't help a new manager, and weekends are normal in retail.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Anyone who likes people could do this, right?

choices.text: What would make a great manager want to run this store?
choices.reply: A loyal team they can build over the next few years, and a real path to running a region, like I did.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive gives you the pitch, and here it's a great one.

choices.text: With a bit of training on our systems, most people who like customers could do it, couldn't they?
choices.why: It undersells the job and doesn't help you find the right person.

choices.text: Isn't it a lot harder than just liking people?
choices.why: Correcting them bluntly discourages a new manager and teaches nothing.

candidates.job: Store manager at a shoe shop
facts: Kept staff for 3 or more years on average

reason.n1: Keeps people and trains them up, just like Hana did. That's what this store needs, inside the range.

view.n1: Mo is the manager I wish I'd had.

candidates.name: Tegan
facts: Hires experienced staff who need little training

reason.n1: Keeps a steady team, but hires experienced people. Hana said the store needs someone who can train brand-new staff.

candidates.name: Jules
candidates.job: Assistant manager at a sports store
facts: Won the company's sales award twice

reason.n1: The most impressive sales record, but hiring 12 people in a year points to a team that keeps leaving. Hana said keeping staff is the real problem.

view.n1: Jules sells. I need someone who keeps people.
